Acknowledgements

I would like to thank Pixoul Gaming for giving me the opportunity to complete an internship centered on a project that combined game design, software architecture, level design, Unity development, testing, and technical documentation. The placement allowed me to study how an entertainment venue connects custom interactive software with VR equipment and physical effects, and then to translate that inspiration into an original prototype.

I am especially grateful to my supervisor, Harout Boyajian, Tech Lead, for being supportive throughout the internship and for trusting me with near-complete freedom over the creative and technical direction of the project. That freedom made the work challenging, but it also allowed me to take responsibility for scope decisions, investigate problems, evaluate alternatives, and learn from the consequences of each iteration.

I also appreciate the support of Abu Dhabi University and the knowledge gained through the Bachelor in Information Technology program. Software Architecture and Design and IT Project Management were particularly valuable because they helped me structure an ambitious idea, defend it through a business case, manage risks, and treat replayability as a quality attribute that needed to influence the whole design rather than one isolated feature.
Summary/Abstract

This report documents an eight-week, 320-hour game-development internship at Pixoul Gaming from June 29 to August 21, 2026. The main project was a Unity prototype for a short-session science-fiction extraction-horror game set in a nuclear facility. The concept was shaped by Pixoul's arcade and VR context: a player should be able to understand the contract quickly, complete meaningful physical work under pressure, leave within a controlled session, and still want to return because the next run changes in vis
ible and understandable ways.

The internship progressed from venue research, concept development, a business case, architecture, risk planning, and backlog preparation into a desktop-first Unity vertical slice. The strongest completed and tracked result was P01 version 0.4.0.0. It combined a three-lobed facility, a fuel-rod recovery and extraction loop, deterministic run variation, and an adversary called the Owl that used bounded, explainable, run-local adaptation rather than machine learning. Recorded delivery evidence for v0.4 includ
ed 28 focused Edit Mode tests, 141 total Edit Mode tests, seven Play Mode tests, a Windows development build, and a 12-second launch smoke check without a recorded project-code exception.

The final two internship weeks began P02, a separate approved-map workstream. I personally drew its floor plan and manually constructed the modular wall shell with prefabs adapted from Creepy Cat's 3D Scifi Kit Starter Kit. By August 21 most rooms were built, while the tracked completion and last wall correction occurred on August 22 and are therefore identified as post-internship continuation. AI agents assisted with planning, analysis, partial code and editor tooling, automated checks, and documentation u

nder my direction and review; they did not author my entire manual P02 shell. The project established strong automated and desktop evidence, but human readability, fairness, XR comfort, headset operation, and physical hardware remained untested. The internship strengthened my commitment to game development and showed me how architecture, project management, evidence discipline, and honest limitation reporting support creative work.

1. Introduction

Internships are valuable because they require students to convert academic knowledge into decisions that have real constraints, stakeholders, deadlines, and consequences. My placement at Pixoul Gaming placed me in a particularly interesting environment: the organization operates a public gaming and immersive-entertainment venue, while the project I proposed required the mindset of a small game-development team. I had to think about the attraction of a concept, the realities of building it in Unity, the oper
ational need for a repeatable arcade session, the safety and comfort of VR, and the evidence needed before calling an experience successful.

The internship ran for eight weeks from June 29 to August 21, 2026, with 40 hours completed each week for a total of 320 hours. I worked under Harout Boyajian, Tech Lead. I did not have a formally confirmed departmental title, so this report describes the placement accurately as game-development work under technical leadership and alongside an R&D context rather than assigning an unsupported organizational label.

The main outcome was a desktop-first Unity extraction-horror prototype. The game's near-future nuclear facility provided a focused setting for a short contract: enter, identify dangerous fuel rods, transport them to the intake, manage an intelligent threat, survive extraction, and leave. The intended product direction was VR and venue-specific physical immersion, but actual headset and hardware access was not established during the recorded period. Therefore, desktop implementation and automated tests serve
d as engineering evidence while XR comfort, physical haptics, and customer experience remained explicit future validation gates.
1.1 Learning Goals

My first learning goal was to experience the full path from an early creative idea to a structured, testable prototype. I wanted to avoid treating game design as a list of attractive features. Instead, I aimed to define a central player promise, identify the risks that could prevent it from working, choose one question for each prototype milestone, and use evidence to decide what to keep, simplify, or defer.

My second goal was to improve my Unity and C# development practice. This included learning how scenes, prefabs, state machines, deterministic seeds, navigation representations, test assemblies, build configurations, and debugging tools fit together. A prefab is a reusable Unity asset that can be instantiated many times with consistent structure [5]. This was especially relevant when I later used a modular environment kit to construct the P02 facility walls.

The third goal was to connect architecture to a commercial quality need. Replayability mattered because Pixoul operates in an arcade-like venue: a one-time experience may be memorable, but a sustainable game should offer a reason to return. I therefore treated replayability as a quality attribute that affected objectives, layout states, route choices, threat behavior, reset reliability, testing, and future content structure. The aim was not unlimited procedural generation. It was controlled variation that r
emained understandable, fair, and testable.

Finally, I wanted to learn how to work responsibly with AI-assisted tools. My supervisor encouraged their use, and I used agents for design drafts, analysis, partial code and editor tooling, test support, and documentation. My learning goal was to remain the project owner: I set direction, made scope decisions, operated Unity, reviewed and corrected outputs, manually constructed the later P02 walls, and distinguished an agent suggestion from verified implementation.
1.2 Learning Activities

The learning activities combined observation, design, implementation, testing, and reflection. I began by touring the venue and researching how custom games could connect Unity software to specialized VR spaces and physical effects. I then produced a living set of Obsidian-compatible project documents: a project hub, vision brief, sprint plan, backlog, risk register, decision log, prototype log, QA template, architecture outline, and implementation handoffs. These documents were not a separate academic exer
cise. They acted as control panels for active decisions and helped prevent later proposals from being mistaken for completed features.

Development proceeded through question-driven milestones. Each milestone protected a baseline, introduced a bounded change, recorded automated evidence, and left human questions open when no participant observation existed. I also reviewed screenshots, scene hierarchies, test results, build behavior, and Git history. In the final two weeks, learning became strongly spatial and manual: I translated my own two-dimensional floor plan into a three-dimensional modular wall shell, corrected scale and connection p
roblems, and learned that a plan can be geometrically clear while still requiring many small construction decisions.
2. Company Description
2.1 About the Company

Pixoul Gaming is located at Al Qana in Abu Dhabi. Its official public description presents it as a 4,500-square-meter virtual-reality and esports hub with five zones, ten VR experiences, an esports academy, gaming broadcast studios, an esports bar, and an esports arena [1], [2]. This combination of public entertainment, competitive gaming, training, and custom immersive experiences made it an appropriate setting for an internship project concerned with both software and physical experience.

During onboarding I was introduced to PC gaming rooms, VR spaces, racing simulators, and custom in-house experiences. I was particularly interested in two open VR areas and in the way an elevator-themed thriller experience used environmental effects such as floor vibration, airflow, and heat to reinforce events inside the game. Other experiences used more specialized physical controls, such as a parachute mechanism that required the player to pull on its sides. These observations made the difference between
venue entertainment and a home game concrete: the room itself can become part of the interface.

The official website describes Pixoul's broader offering as covering VR, retro, console, mobile, and esports zones and connects the venue with game development and education as well as public entertainment [2]. The venue opened at Al Qana in November 2022 [3]. My report uses those public facts only for general context. Internal company structure, client lists, and development processes are not inferred beyond my own placement experience.
2.2 Organizational Layout and Internship Context

I worked under Harout Boyajian, Tech Lead, and sat near a member of R&D. I was not given a formal departmental designation that I can verify, and I did not work across the wider corporate hierarchy. The most accurate description is therefore that I completed an individual game-development project under technical supervision, with exposure to the relationship between research, software development, venue hardware, and operations.

The project structure was deliberately intern-led. My supervisor gave me near-complete freedom over the creative and technical direction, subject to the project needing to make sense for Pixoul. This freedom was important because it required me to justify the idea, define a practical slice, report progress, and accept when a promising feature was too risky for the available evidence. The working relationship was less about receiving a fixed list of programming tasks and more about proposing, structuring, an
d delivering a coherent prototype while keeping the supervisor informed.
2.2.1 Visitors and Stakeholders

Pixoul serves professional and amateur gamers and offers experiences that range from individual VR attractions to multiplayer, console, training, and esports activities [1], [2]. For my project, this created several implied stakeholders: the player, the venue operator who must start and reset a session reliably, the technical team responsible for software and hardware integration, and management evaluating

whether the concept offers repeat value. No customer study was performed during the internship, so these stakeholder needs were design assumptions and architecture drivers rather than measured customer findings.
2.3 Company History and Venue Relevance

Pixoul announced the venue in 2022 as an integrated VR and esports destination and opened at Al Qana on November 4 of that year [3]. By the time of my 2026 placement, its public offering combined commercial attractions with custom immersive technology. The venue context influenced my central design decision: the prototype should not be a long home-style campaign that depends on many hours of progression. It should be a self-contained contract that can be explained, played, reset, and replayed within a contr
olled session.

This arcade requirement made retention and replayability important without justifying an oversized feature list. A returning player should encounter a different combination of routes, objective positions, hazards, or threat pressures while still understanding the rules. This became the bridge between company relevance and my academic work in architecture: replayability was treated as a quality attribute with system-wide consequences.
3. Internship Activities
3.1 Training and Week 1 Concept Development

The onboarding period was short but enjoyable. I toured the venue, learned about the different gaming areas, and researched how the custom experiences combined software with physical equipment. The most important outcome was not a list of devices; it was a clearer understanding that haptics and room effects should communicate an in-world meaning. Floor vibration, wind, heat, or a physical control can be memorable, but if several effects mean the same thing—or one effect means too many things—the player may
become confused.

My early brainstorming moved through several ideas before reaching a VR horror extraction roguelike direction. I was attracted to horror because physical effects could reinforce tension, and to extraction play because it creates a clear job, rising risk, and a satisfying exit. I also explored a heart-rate sensor as a possible input to a game mechanic. Later risk analysis showed why raw heart rate should not directly determine detection or failure: sensor noise, individual anxiety, calibration, accessibility
, consent, and positive feedback loops could make the game unfair. The idea was therefore retained as future research with a simulated fallback rather than claimed as an implemented feature.

The Week 1 concept was intentionally broad. Details such as the final three-rod objective, bounded Owl adaptation, three-lobed map, and P02 floor plan were developed later. This chronology matters because it shows genuine iteration rather than presenting the final design as if it existed from the first day.
3.2 Week 2 Planning, Business Case, and Architecture

During Week 2 I converted the concept into a planning spine. I used a business-case and proposal approach from IT Project Management to convince my supervisor that the project was ambitious but manageable if it was divided into prototypes. The Sprint 01 plan defined a single question: could a small VR facility feel tense and understandable while the player located an objective, sensed a threat, and extracted? The plan also created explicit must-have, should-have, could-have, and won't-have boundaries [8].

The Obsidian vault became the center of the planning workflow. The project hub recorded the current phase, assumptions, and open questions. The vision brief connected Pixoul's venue context to a 15-20 minute contract structure. The backlog separated production, core gameplay, threat, run variation, hardware, QA, and communication. The risk register documented failure conditions and fallbacks. A ClickUp-ready task pack translated the plan into actionable work. A first-person design workbook captured rough id
eas about player fantasy, haptic meanings, objectives, the Owl, and the desired reaction after a run: the player should want to play again.

Software architecture helped turn replayability into design constraints. The game would not generate arbitrary runtime geometry. Instead, a deterministic seed would select among authored sockets, route states, lighting conditions, and bounded threat profiles. A deterministic seed is an input that causes the

same choices to be produced again, which helps debugging and testing. The architecture separated the player, interaction, session state, objective, threat, run configuration, and hardware seams [9]. This meant the desktop prototype could use simulated devices while preserving interfaces for later XR or venue hardware.

3.3 Project Definition and Design Objectives

The resulting game direction was a near-future science-fiction extraction-horror experience in which a contractor accepts dangerous short jobs. The internship prototype focused on one contract: enter a damaged nuclear facility, identify three live fuel rods, transport them to an intake, survive the Owl, complete a timed extraction cycle, and cross the open exit. The contractor fantasy gave the player agency and a clear reason to be in the facility; the horror came from incomplete information and an intellig
ent pursuer rather than from graphic violence.

The current slice used three active rods because repeated trips created route decisions and escalating exposure. The Geiger counter supported searching, while scan/acceptance rules distinguished correct rods. Run variation came from seeded objective placements, route states, threat configuration, and other authored choices. This produced procedural feeling without the risk of generating broken geometry. The design also protected rapid reset because an arcade operator needs a reliable way to start the next s
ession.

The design pillars were venue-only immersion, dangerous contract fantasy, replayable uncertainty, an adaptive adversary, and comfort/reliability. These were ideals rather than completed validation results. For example, the vision targeted a physical effect, but real haptic hardware was unavailable in the recorded evidence. The report therefore treats the hardware ambition as a design driver and limitation, not as a delivered feature.
3.4 Game and Systems Design

The Owl was designed to appear intelligent without depending on machine learning. Its behavior used a state machine: a controlled set of modes such as patrolling, investigating, pursuing, and recovering, with explicit conditions for movement between them. It also stored bounded run-local evidence about player behavior. For example, repeated route tendencies could bias later patrol choices. The adaptation was deterministic, explainable, capped, and cleared when the run reset. It did not train on customers, r
emember players across sessions, or autonomously invent behavior.

This distinction supported both fairness and engineering. A venue operator and developer need to be able to explain why the entity chose a route, reproduce a problematic run, and disable adaptation for comparison. The project therefore kept an operator overlay and seed controls. The player-facing ambition was that the Owl would pressure repeated tactics while leaving credible counterplay: break sight, change routes, manage sound, use cover, and create distractions. Automated rules could verify priorities an
d thresholds, but only human observation could establish whether these responses felt fair.

Replayability also influenced content architecture. The broader product direction allowed curated combinations of sites, objectives, entities, and conditions, but the internship protected one nuclear contract. Compatibility would be authored rather than assuming every module could combine with every other module. This reduced combinatorial testing and allowed each physical effect to keep a narrow meaning. It also demonstrated a key project-management lesson: a scalable concept begins by proving one complete
example, not by constructing a generalized system before its player value is known.
3.5 Weeks 3-4: Unity Vertical Slice and Prototype 1

Weeks 3 and 4 moved from planning into Unity implementation. The initial vertical slice established a desktop player, facility greybox, interaction system, fuel-rod objective, intake and extraction states, threat behavior, run configuration, debugging support, and automated tests. Desktop controls were used because target XR hardware and runtime were not confirmed. This was a deliberate evidence layer: it allowed rapid testing of contract logic and navigation without pretending to validate headset comfort o
r physical interaction.

The scene was built as a greybox, meaning a simplified environment used to test size, routes, interactions, and pacing before final art. Early versions emphasized functional completeness. Later Week 4 work improved route readability, interactions, environment presentation, fullscreen behavior, and versioning. A run-local adaptation system was introduced without allowing it to override more credible information. Sight, sound, route knowledge, and adaptation needed clear priority rules so the Owl would not ap
pear omniscient.

Several technical problems became useful learning moments. Movement sometimes disappeared at high refresh rates because individual movement steps fell below `CharacterController.minMoveDistance`; setting the threshold to zero removed that loss. OpenXR startup without a headset required build-time configuration handling rather than a claim that XR itself had been tested. Changes around XR initialization also needed to preserve whether a rod was currently
held. Procedural footsteps initially sounded too harsh and were softened, but their final perceptual quality was not established by a later human test.

By the end of Week 4, the project had a functioning prototype family and a stronger process for protecting previous behavior through tests. It was still not a finished game. Visual fidelity, first-time comprehension, pacing, fairness, XR comfort, haptics, and real customer desire to replay remained open.
3.6 Week 5: v0.3 Readable Stealth and Counterplay

Version 0.3.0.0 narrowed the development question to readable stealth and contractor counterplay. The milestone strengthened how the Owl interpreted confirmed sight, sound, and last-known information, and it introduced portable or fixed distractions without allowing a weak stimulus to erase a more credible target. Graded footsteps and restrained investigation cues were intended to expose cause and effect through the world rather than requiring a permanent stealth meter [12].

The delivery was supported by exact recorded evidence: 22 of 22 focused Edit Mode tests, 133 of 133 total Edit Mode tests, and six of six Play Mode tests passed. Unity's Edit Mode tests run in the Editor and can exercise game and editor code, while Play Mode tests exercise behavior in the runtime context [4]. The v0.3 Windows development build also completed and launched through its recorded smoke window. A smoke test is a short check that the application starts and remains alive; it is not a complete playt
hrough or proof of experience quality.

These results showed that documented rules and integration cases behaved as expected at delivery. They did not show that an uninformed player understood noise, cover, distractions, or the Owl's adaptation. The human-validation sheet remained open, which is why the report uses “recorded automated validation” rather than “fully tested.”
3.7 Week 6: v0.4 Spatial Readability

Version 0.4.0.0 protected the v0.3 gameplay baseline while replacing the map with a stronger spatial experiment. The selected 7C layout used three unequal lobes around an inaccessible central void, joined by three pairwise connectors. Each lobe had a different identity and one objective pocket, while the connectors offered different risk and visibility patterns. The goal was to help the player form a mental map and make deliberate route choices under pursuit [13], [14].

The layout was represented declaratively before the scene was generated. In this context, declarative topology means that rooms, nodes, links, objective relationships, and route requirements were expressed as data or inspectable rules rather than existing only as manually placed geometry. Automated tests could therefore ask whether every objective had the required graph-distinct routes, whether connectors were used correctly, and whether the previous gameplay systems remained integrated.

The milestone still had an important limitation. Automated topology tests could prove graph relationships, object presence, and documented integration cases, but they could not prove that a new player recognized the lobes, understood the connectors, felt the Owl was fair, or remained comfortable in VR. These outcomes required uninformed human and headset testing that was not completed.

The final two internship weeks started P02, a separate approved-map workstream. I personally drew the floor plan and used it as the locked topology reference. Unlike P01's generated greybox, P02 translated a hand-drawn plan into a modular environment assembled from reusable wall, corner, doorway, floor, and structural prefabs. The exercise shifted the project from systems-first proof toward detailed level construction.

The environment used Creepy Cat's 3D Scifi Kit Starter Kit, distributed through the Unity Asset Store under the Standard Unity Asset Store EULA [6], [7]. I did not model the imported kit from scratch. My work was to select and import the pack, understand its modular dimensions, adapt it to the plan, place the wall pieces manually, and create or adjust custom transition pieces where the available modules could not express the required angles cleanly.

Translation required a consistent scale. The facility-kit documentation recorded a working conversion of 0.025 meters per plan pixel, a 0.30-meter wall thickness, and a 3.60-meter wall height [15]. Those numbers helped align the drawing with reusable prefabs, but they did not eliminate manual judgment. Corners that looked simple in two dimensions could produce overlaps or gaps in Unity.

Mirrored pieces changed collider and orientation behavior. Small angle errors accumulated across long walls. Door openings needed enough clearance, and hierarchy organization had to remain understandable as the shell grew.

Week 7 produced the facility-kit groundwork and the first manually authored rooms: the Entrance, Room 2, and Room 3. Week 8 expanded the shell through most of the plan and involved repeated corrections to wall angle, thickness, connection, and hierarchy. The Git history records “a few left to go” on August 21. The commits that recorded “rooms done” and a forgotten-wall correction were made on August 22, so the report does not move them backward into the official 320 hours.

AI-assisted tools contributed to the surrounding workflow. Agents helped draft implementation prompts, analyze map fidelity, suggest editor tooling and tests, and automate disposable facility-kit, collider, or integration layers. The manual P02 wall shell itself was my work. This distinction is important because the presence of a generator or prompt in the repository does not mean it authored all visible geometry. The report separates manual wall construction, imported art, custom transition pieces, and lat
er automated integration by ownership and date.
3.9 Technical Implementation in Unity

The Unity project used C# components for the player, objectives, interactions, threat behavior, run configuration, feedback, testing, and editor automation. The architecture favored narrow responsibilities and interfaces. Session state controlled the current run; seeded configuration selected authored variations; objective components handled rod and extraction rules; the Owl used a state machine plus bounded evidence; and feedback or hardware-facing systems sat behind replaceable seams. This reduced direct
dependencies and made it possible to test rules without loading every scene.

The project used both Unity's NavMesh and a fallback route-graph concept. A NavMesh is a surface representation used to calculate where an agent can walk. A route graph represents important locations and connections more abstractly. Structural checks could confirm that navigation data or graph routes existed, but they could not guarantee that the Owl traversed them naturally in every encounter. This distinction became more important in P02, where a large manual shell, generated colliders, and later populati
on work increased the chance that a technically connected route might still be awkward.

Editor tooling was used when repetitive operations needed to be reproducible and disposable. A generator could create a known hierarchy, while validation code checked ownership and counts. The current P02 wall-collider generator, for example, was designed to create separate collider children rather than editing imported prefab assets. However, its present source and related P02 tests are modified or untracked, and no current passing test run was recorded during this report audit. Those source assertions are
therefore not presented as completed validation.
3.10 Testing, Debugging, and Build Evidence

Testing was organized in layers. Focused Edit Mode suites checked the current milestone's narrow rules. The full Edit Mode suite protected broader systems and editor-generation invariants. Play Mode tests exercised runtime integration in Unity's play context. Windows development builds then checked that the standalone player could be produced, and launch smoke checks looked for immediate startup failure. Each layer answered a different question, so passing one did not replace the others.

Debugging depended on reproducibility. Seeds allowed a run to be repeated, operator telemetry exposed state and evidence, and tests recorded the expected priority of sight, sound, adaptation, and reset behavior. Build smoke evidence was described narrowly because a 12-second stable launch does not show that a 15-minute session is fun, readable, or free from later defects.

Human evidence remained the largest gap. No recorded uninformed-player results established mental-map formation, counterplay comprehension, fairness, fear, fun, or desire to replay. No headset evidence established VR scale, locomotion comfort, reach, throwing, crouch fatigue, spatial audio, or safety. No physical hardware evidence established heat, airflow, floor vibration, haptics, or heart-rate behavior. Maintaining these “Not Tested” labels was part of the quality process rather than an admission that th
e automated work had no value.

3.11 Documentation and Project Management

The project used a weekly, question-driven agile rhythm. Planning identified one prototype goal and the risks that could invalidate it. Implementation and local checks occurred during the week. Evidence, captures, decision logs, and handoffs were then updated so the next iteration started from a known baseline. This reduced the chance that a future agent—or I myself—would act on an attractive but superseded idea.

Git history provided a dated record of deliverables and manual P02 progress. It also exposed limits. P01 v0.4 was tracked and build-validated, while P02 remained a mix of tracked manual work, modified scene/settings, and untracked later tools and captures. For the report audit I treated all working-tree changes as user-owned and did not reset, clean, stage, commit, push, run Unity, or produce a new game build.

Project documentation also supported handoff. The current implementation state, predecessor work, known risks, facility-kit rules, v0.3 and v0.4 scopes, and human-validation sheets gave later work a clear evidence boundary. The documents did not make every proposal true; they made it easier to state what was approved, implemented, automatically checked, observed, or still unknown.

4. Overall Internship Experience
4.1 Technical Skills

The internship expanded my technical understanding beyond writing individual scripts. I learned to think about how gameplay state, scene construction, reusable prefabs, run configuration, navigation, tests, and build settings interact. Problems often appeared at the boundary between systems: a movement threshold depended on frame timing; an XR initialization change could affect held-object state; a wall prefab's orientation affected collider ownership; and a graph that was structurally connected could still
produce poor traversal.

I also learned the value of deterministic and explainable systems. The Owl could have been described vaguely as “learning the player,” but a bounded run-local model was better for the prototype. It gave the impression of adaptation while remaining testable and debuggable. The seed system served a similar purpose by allowing variation without losing reproducibility. These choices made the technical implementation support the intended player experience instead of becoming complexity for its own sake.

Manual P02 construction developed a different technical skill. I had to reason about scale, pivots, angles, wall thickness, doorway dimensions, hierarchy, and modular reuse. The floor plan remained an authority, but implementing it required interpreting how two-dimensional lines become three-dimensional occupied space. This work made level design feel less like drawing rooms and more like managing spatial constraints.
4.2 Professional Skills

The strongest professional lesson was ownership. My supervisor's trust meant that I could not wait for every task to be prescribed. I needed to propose the work, explain its value, identify risks, choose a feasible milestone, and report honestly when evidence was incomplete. The business case and planning spine helped establish this responsibility at the start of the internship.

I improved at maintaining traceable decisions. Scope changes were recorded, test counts were attached to the correct version, and P01 was kept separate from the unfinished P02 workstream. This discipline matters when a project has many documents and AI-assisted outputs, because polished wording can otherwise hide that an idea was only proposed. I learned to ask: what is the primary evidence, when was it produced, who performed the work, and what does it actually prove?

Another professional skill was accepting limited evidence. It would have been easy to describe passing tests as proof that the level was readable or the game was complete. Instead, I learned that reporting an open human-validation gate protects the project. It tells the next developer or stakeholder what kind of work is required rather than encouraging them to trust the wrong result.
4.3 Soft Skills
The project improved my communication because the idea had to make sense to both technical and non-technical readers. I practiced explaining an extraction loop, state machine, deterministic seed,

NavMesh, prefab workflow, and test evidence without relying only on class names. Handoff documents also required me to state boundaries precisely so another person or agent could continue without reopening every decision.

Creative freedom strengthened decision-making. I considered many interesting mechanics—heart rate, physical heat, wind, floor vibration, broader contract combinations, recovery systems, equipment, and more—but learned that saying “not yet” can protect the core idea. The risk register gave those decisions a professional form: a delayed feature was not forgotten; it had a reason, trigger, and fallback.

The internship also improved patience and problem solving. Manual modular construction involved repeated corrections that were not glamorous but were necessary for a coherent shell. Technical debugging sometimes required preserving state, restarting after editor instability, or separating a configuration symptom from a gameplay defect. These experiences made the final outcome feel earned through iteration rather than produced by one successful attempt.
4.4 University Applied Knowledge

Software Architecture and Design was the most useful university course for this project. It taught me how quality attributes influence architecture and how a niche attribute can still be analyzed systematically even if it is not a standard textbook example. I applied that approach to replayability. For Pixoul, replayability was connected to customer return and arcade value, so it could not be treated as a random-number feature added at the end.

Replayability influenced the architecture through deterministic seeds, authored variable states, isolated run configuration, reusable contract concepts, reset behavior, and bounded adaptation. It also influenced quality assurance: variations needed to preserve a valid critical path and be reproducible when a defect appeared. At the design level, it encouraged route choice and meaningful uncertainty. At the project level, it warned against fully procedural geometry and unrestricted module combinations that c
ould create too much content and testing scope.

IT Project Management was the second major connection. I used a business case and proposal to obtain support for the project, then used sprint goals, a backlog, risk responses, priorities, acceptance criteria, cut lines, stakeholder updates, and versioned evidence to pace the work. These tools helped me start a large project without pretending that the whole vision could be delivered in eight weeks.
4.5 Career Influence

The internship made me more certain that I want to continue in game development. I enjoyed the combination of creative direction and technical structure: deciding what the player should feel, translating that into systems and spaces, debugging when reality disagreed with the idea, and then using evidence to decide what changed next.

The most difficult challenge was replayability and my concern about player retention. It was not solved by one mechanic, and the internship did not include a customer-retention study. The useful outcome was learning how to turn the concern into practical architecture and testable decisions. A

repeatable arcade game needs a clear first experience, a reliable reset, visible variation, understandable rules, and enough uncertainty to make a second attempt meaningful. Future human testing must determine whether the current prototype actually produces that desire.

The experience also showed me the type of developer I want to become. I want to be capable of owning a design problem across code, architecture, level layout, validation, and communication while remaining honest about work assisted by tools or created by third parties. The project is unfinished as a product, but it gave me a strong foundation for continuing in technical game development and design.
5. Conclusion

The eight-week placement at Pixoul Gaming transformed an early interest in venue haptics and VR horror into a structured Unity prototype and a documented development process. I began with onboarding and research, used a business case and architecture planning to control an ambitious concept, implemented and validated successive P01 milestones, and ended the official internship by translating my own approved floor plan into a mostly constructed manual P02 wall shell.

P01 v0.4.0.0 is the strongest completed outcome. It preserved the extraction loop and readable-stealth systems inside a three-lobed facility and has recorded evidence for 28 focused Edit Mode tests, 141 total Edit Mode tests, seven Play Mode tests, a Windows development build, and a 12-second launch smoke check. P02 is separate: it demonstrates manual level-design and modular-construction learning, but its tracked completion occurred on August 22 and its later integration remains unfinished.

The central lesson was that creative ambition benefits from evidence discipline. Tests, builds, logs, Git history, captures, and handoffs made progress traceable, but none replaced human or headset validation. The project did not establish player readability, fairness, comfort, physical haptic quality, heart-rate behavior, or customer retention. These are the correct next questions, together with completing P02 integration and testing on target venue hardware.

The internship strengthened my intention to work in game development. It allowed me to connect Software Architecture and Design, IT Project Management, Unity development, level construction, AI-assisted workflows, and professional reporting in one project. Most importantly, it taught me to protect authorship and truth: credit imported assets, describe AI assistance accurately, preserve my own manual work, attach claims to the right milestone, and state “not tested” when the necessary evidence does not exist

Appendix A. Technical Terms Used in the Report
Term
Plain-language meaning in this project
Build smoke test
A short startup check used to confirm that a standalone build launches and does not immediately fail. It is not a complete playthrough.
Declarative topology
A representation of rooms, nodes, links, and constraints as inspectable data or rules rather than only as scene geometry.
Deterministic seed
An input that reproduces the same authored selections, allowing a variable run to be debugged and tested again.
Edit Mode test
A Unity test executed in the Editor context, suitable for rules, data, editor tooling, and many generation checks.
Greybox
A simplified environment used to validate scale, layout, interactions, navigation, and pacing before final art.
NavMesh
A navigable-surface representation used by game agents to calculate movement through a scene.
Play Mode test
A Unity test that exercises selected behavior in the runtime/play context.
Prefab
A reusable Unity asset whose instances share a defined structure, useful for modular objects such as walls and doors.
Raycast
A query projected through the scene to detect what a player or system is pointing at or can see, usually through colliders.
State machine
A controlled set of behavior states and explicit rules for moving between them.
